title: Teach Microduck to score a goal
text: What you will build  The final scene contains one Microduck, one football, and one goal. The robot must find the ball, locate the goal, approach a useful kicking position, make contact, and recover its stance. You will learn what each part of this system does and how the parts work together.    1 Understand the mechanism   2 Control and train   3 See and navigate   4 Score autonomously     By the end, you can   Explain how joints, actuators, observations, actions, and rewards relate.  Launch a Newton / Isaac Lab simulation and inspect a fixed policy in action.  Run a bounded training exercise, locate checkpoints, and interpret training curves.  Connect camera detections, ToF ranges, and body attitude to autonomous task states.  Record both successes and failures, distinguishing model metrics from task metrics. title: Mechanism and control timing
text: From assembly to components  Microduck is a small biped. Its legs support and move the body, the neck directs its view, and the trunk houses computing, power, and connections. Visual meshes describe appearance. Joints and collision geometry describe permitted motion and contact. These play different roles in simulation.       Open interactive model    Assembled   Exploded  Reset view    Click a part or its label to inspect it  Left-drag to orbit, middle-drag to pan, scroll or pinch to zoom. Use the slider to separate the parts.    Move the separation slider to inspect the leg and head servos. Click their labels to identify the driven joints, then inspect the camera, controller board and battery. Reset to trace the leg joints.   Hardware revision and simulation joints  There are 15 servos: five per leg, four for the head and neck, and one for the beak. The policy drives 14 joints; the beak remains fixed. The CAD retains a Raspberry Pi Zero 2 W board mesh; this is not the current Beta RK3566 electronics configuration. Chapter 6 introduces the simulated sensors.     Parts, joints, and degrees of freedom  A pen held at its tip can rotate in several directions, while a hinge normally rotates around one fixed axis. Robot joints impose similar constraints. A degree of freedom is an independent variable needed to describe permitted motion; a component count describes physical pieces. The 70 components in this viewer do not imply 70 policy actions.      Region  Active joints  Main role      Each leg  Hip yaw, roll, pitch; knee; ankle: 5 joints  Support the body and place the foot    Neck and head  Neck pitch; head pitch, yaw, roll: 4 joints  Orient the camera and head    Beak  Physical servo; not controlled by this policy  Shown in 3D model, excluded from the 14-action interface      Select a hip servo and inspect its output shaft and nearby bearing. The servo controls an active angle, the bearing supports rotation, and brackets connect adjacent joints. Material, shape, and assembly clearance affect motion. The viewer preserves 3D model detail but does not simulate screw preload, plastic elasticity, or cable forces; it is an anatomy aid rather than manufacturing documentation.    How software moves the mechanism    1 Policy action   2 Joint targets   3 Actuator torque   4 Physics update   5 New observation   A policy does not teleport the robot to a desired position. It outputs actions that become joint targets. Actuators produce torque based on the difference between target and measured state. The resulting motion depends on contact, gravity, inertia, and friction.  The policy runs at 50 Hz and physics at 200 Hz: each action spans four physics steps. Backlash introduces passive joints representing transmission play. Passive joints are not additional policy outputs.    Describe motion with frames      Frame  What is expressed here      World  Pitch, goal, and overall robot position    Body  Forward, lateral, and turn commands; ball relative to the robot    Camera  Image rays and detected target directions    Joint-local  A joint’s axis and angle       Check your understanding  If the head joints stay fixed, is the camera image necessarily stable?   Show explanation  No. Body pitch and roll move the neck and camera. Image stability depends on camera orientation relative to the world, not only on joint angles.      Exercise: trace one load path  Start with the assembled model. Trace a path from the left foot through the ankle, shin, knee, thigh, and hip. Ground support reaches the body through this chain. Explode the assembly and select the servos and brackets around a joint. Identify the fixed housing and the part driven by its output. Explosion offsets are display positions, not physically reachable joint poses.  A servo combines a motor, reduction gears, position feedback, and control electronics. Reaching a target takes time and is limited by torque, speed, friction, and backlash. A policy issuing an angle does not mean the joint instantly reaches it. Chapter 2 observes this difference; Chapter 3 explains how a policy learns around it.   Check your understanding  Does moving the foot farther out in the exploded view change the simulated leg length?   Show explanation  No. The web view explains components. Robot description files define simulated dimensions and joint connections.      What the policy receives and produces  Chapter 1 runs inference with a trained policy. It maps the current observation to 14 joint actions without updating neural-network parameters. Changing the velocity command tests the same model under a different request; it is not training. Choosing a different model file changes the policy. title: Learning to walk
text:
One reinforcement-learning loop  The policy receives a vector containing body attitude, angular velocity, joint state, a velocity command, and the previous action. It outputs joint actions, physics advances, and rewards measure progress toward the objective. PPO collects a batch of interactions, updates the policy, and samples again.    1 Observe   2 Sample actions   3 Simulate   4 Compute rewards   5 Update PPO   The environment count is the number of simultaneous robot copies. Iterations repeat collection and optimization. More environments increase parallel sampling and memory demand. A rising training reward means the optimized objective is improving; independent behavior checks are still necessary.    Why PPO looks beyond immediate reward  Lifting a foot can briefly reduce stability while being necessary for forward progress. Reinforcement learning therefore considers return over time rather than just the current reward. A discount factor reduces the weight of more distant rewards, balancing immediate feedback with longer-term consequences.  In PPO, the actor chooses actions and the critic estimates future return. An outcome better than the critic expected receives a positive advantage estimate, encouraging a higher probability for the corresponding action; a worse outcome does the opposite. PPO limits how far an update moves from the old policy to reduce abrupt changes. It does not guarantee that every update improves real task success.  A critic may receive additional simulation information to evaluate trajectories, but the deployed actor must depend only on observations available at runtime. A simulator knowing exact body velocity does not imply that hardware has a perfect velocity sensor. Keep training or scoring ground truth out of the deployed controller.  When designing rewards, list desired behaviors and then consider shortcuts. Rewarding ball motion may encourage body collisions; rewarding stillness may discourage walking. Track both goals and constraints: velocity error, episode length, falls, joint limits, and contact type. This chapter practices the training loop; Chapter 7 tests the complete task definition.    Run a short training exercise    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 64 \
  --iterations 20 \
  --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-01    This is a workflow exercise, not a promise that 20 iterations will learn to walk. Expected result: terminal progress, a new run directory, checkpoints, and an exported policy. Observe loss, return, and episode length without committing to a long training run.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py tensorboard \
  --logdir outputs/student-walk-01 \
  --port 6006    Open the local TensorBoard address printed in the terminal. Compare reward with episode length. If reward grows while episodes remain short, consider whether the objective rewards a brief action followed by a fall.  Current practice uses full-body contacts, including the head and legs during falls. New outputs are separate experiments; historical learning curves retain their original configuration. Training does not render frames; policy playback uses the shared RTX lighting and materials.    From a smoke run to a longer training run  The 20-iteration exercise checks the pipeline, not convergence. A longer run below uses 1024 environments for 2500 iterations in a new output directory. Judge convergence with curves and independent evaluation, not iteration count alone.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-walk \
  --num-envs 1024 --iterations 2500 --seed 101 \
  --output outputs/walking-training-01    Use TensorBoard to compare reward, episode length, falls and velocity error. Use the short-run export in the next section, or explicitly select outputs/walking-training-01/exported/policy.onnx after this longer run. Neither changes the official model.    Explicitly test your own policy  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model outputs/student-walk-01/exported/policy.onnx \
  --velocity 0.30 0.00 0.00 \
  --seconds 12 \
  --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/student-walk-test-01    Here you deliberately select your own model. Compare support, drift, and falls with the official model from Chapter 1. Later lessons still use  models/walk.onnx ; this export does not change their default.   Go further  To increase the budget, choose a new output directory and try, for example, 1,024 environments and 500 iterations. Check available memory and time first. A saved checkpoint is not a qualification result. Evaluate unseen seeds and retain failures.     Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py walk \
  --model models/walk.onnx --velocity 0.3 0 0 \
  --seconds 12 --seed 202 \
  --output outputs/official-walk-comparison-01    Match command, duration and seed. Compare falls, distance and actual velocity, then test standing at zero command. One moving demonstration is not a complete skill benchmark.    Why domain randomization matters  Real actuators do not have identical friction, delay, and backlash on every run. Varying parameters in training exposes the policy to more conditions. A narrow range can overfit; an excessively broad range can make learning difficult. Randomization can improve robustness but does not replace hardware testing.   Check your understanding  Why is the highest-reward training episode not an independent test?   Show explanation  It contributed to learning or selection, and reward may differ from task success. Independent testing uses predetermined scenarios and success criteria and counts every outcome.      Checkpoints, curves, and independent tests  Practice starts from random parameters rather than the course walking weights. Each PPO iteration gathers trajectories from several environments and then updates the policy. Rewards combine velocity tracking, body attitude, action smoothness, and contact-related terms. Two policies with similar total rewards may obtain them through accurate motion or simply moving less; inspect both behavior and individual reward terms.   initial.pt  records initialization;  model_*.pt  files are checkpoints;  env.yaml  and  agent.yaml  preserve environment and optimizer settings;  exported/policy.onnx  is the inference export. A checkpoint can contain optimizer state, while ONNX normally preserves the inference graph. They are not interchangeable file formats.  Record the training budget, held-out test seeds, and observed behavior. The 20-iteration exercise teaches sampling, updates, saving, and export. A weak practice policy is no reason to replace downstream course defaults. For a larger budget, keep the earlier run, use a new output directory, and state whether you changed environment count, iteration count, or rewards.   Check your understanding  Does saving only ONNX guarantee an exact training continuation?   Show explanation  No. Exact continuation also needs optimizer, normalization and random states, together with matching configuration. Preserve full checkpoints and training settings.      Will a flat-ground skill handle a slope?  You can now collect rollouts, update PPO, export ONNX and test a policy. Will its foot clearance and balance adjustments work on a slope? Predict the outcome, then test the same policy in Chapter 4.

title: Adapt walking to slopes
text:
Start with a testable question  Do not assume the old actor will fail. Hold the policy, command, duration, friction and initial-state distribution fixed while varying slope. Test traversal and balance, not just a single attractive frame.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Terrain generalization  Baseline：Same actor: flat/up/down；Isaac Lab training：Sample parallel terrains；Held-out evaluation：Arrival, falls, speed error       Terrain generalization     Baseline  Same actor: flat/up/down   Isaac Lab training  Sample parallel terrains   Held-out evaluation  Arrival, falls, speed  error    Evaluate before adapting. Retain flat-ground ability while testing improvements on slopes.     Build a flat–ramp–landing scene  The surface has a 0.35 m flat approach, a 1 m horizontal ramp, and a landing. Positive angles ascend; negative angles descend. A continuous collision mesh avoids unintended steps. Visual materials do not determine contact dynamics.      The darker surface marks the ramp; gold guides show direction and green marks the target. These visual markings do not change contact physics.              Flat: 0.35 m  Ramp run: 1 m  Landing      h(x) = tan(α) · clip(x − 0.35, 0, 1)    Slope α / °       Adjust the slope to compare ascent and descent. Horizontal and vertical scales match; the landing height changes with the angle.    坡面高度  \[h(x)=\tan(\alpha)\,\operatorname{clip}(x-0.35,0,1)\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    slope = math.tan(math.radians(cfg.slope_deg))
xs = [-48.0, 2.35, 3.35, 52.0]
zs = [0.0, 0.0, slope, slope]
vertices = [(x, y, z) for x, z in zip(xs, zs) for y in [-48.0, 52.0]]
origin = np.array([2.0, 2.0, 0.0])    The mesh origin is (2, 2, 0). Subtracting it places the robot at relative x = 0 and the ramp between x = 0.35 m and 1.35 m. Continuous approach and landing support extends across 100 × 100 m so failures do not fall off a small terrain tile. Isaac Lab’s TerrainGenerator and TerrainImporter share this geometry across visualization, physics tests and parallel training.    Test the official walking policy first  Run the official walking policy on a 5° uphill ramp for 20 seconds. Run the command below from the repository root with a new output directory.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --slope 5 --num-envs 1 --seconds 20 --seed 42001 \
  --output outputs/slope-up-05    Without --headless this opens Isaac Sim. Use --num-envs 5 --headless for batched evaluation, and test 0, ±5, ±10 and ±15 degrees in separate output directories. The first 2 s are standing; then the command is 0.25 m/s. Actual speed may differ.  Success requires reaching x ≥ 1.45 m within 20 s with lateral error below 0.3 m and staying upright throughout. A fall remains a failure even if the body later slides across the finish. Reports separate reaching, falls and velocity RMSE.      Slope  Pass  Fall      0°  5/5  0/5    +5°  0/5  0/5    -5°  0/5  5/5    +10°  0/5  0/5    -10°  0/5  5/5    +15°  0/5  0/5    -15°  0/5  5/5      Each angle uses five lightly perturbed starts. Flat trials pass; uphill trials stall without falling; downhill trials fall. This small baseline identifies an adaptation need, not general reliability.    Why flat-ground experience may not transfer  A slope changes foot clearance, gravity along the surface and usable friction. Insufficient clearance or propulsion can stall ascent; downhill landing and balance changes can cause falls. Survival alone misses stalled traversal.    Continue learning across terrain types  Keep the official ONNX unchanged. Initialize a new actor from its weights and normalization, with a fresh critic and optimizer. Mix 25% flat terrain with ascending and descending terrain. Verify initial actor parity before learning.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-terrain \
  --model models/walk.onnx \
  --num-envs 256 --iterations 1000 --seed 43001 \
  --output outputs/terrain-training-01    Training slopes are tan(α), not degrees: 0.03–0.22 is about 1.7°–12.4°. Training uses pyramidal and inverted slopes; evaluation uses straight ramps and separate seeds.    Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    sub_terrains = {

Current practice runs use the same full-contact robot as the demonstrations, so their contact configuration differs from the historical training and defines a new experiment. Training is physics-only; inspect exported policies in the shared RTX scene.    Balance and direction both matter   第一步：定义有物理含义的误差  \[e_{\omega}=\omega_z-\omega_z^*,\qquad u=\frac{e_{\omega}}{\sigma}\]    第二步：把误差转换为平滑、有界的奖励  \[r_{\omega}=\exp(-u^2)=\exp\!\left[-\left(\frac{\omega_z-\omega_z^*}{0.15}\right)^2\right]\]     Python · 核心代码节选  Full source ↗    def yaw_rate_tracking(env, std=0.15):
    # Match the commanded turn rate without penalizing normal roll/pitch motion.
    velocity = env.scene["robot"].data.root_link_ang_vel_b.torch
    target = env.command_manager.get_command("base_velocity")[:, 2]

    # Squared, normalized error gives a symmetric reward in (0, 1].
    return torch.exp(-((velocity[:, 2] - target) / std).square())

title: Explore community movement skills
text: What else can the same robot learn?  Community projects train jumping and ball balancing using different tasks, rewards and initial states. These demonstrations come from their original simulation environments and do not establish equivalent Newton or hardware performance.      Community jump demonstration in the original four-times slow motion. Observe takeoff, flight, landing and the standing handoff.       Community ball-balancing demonstration: watch the moving support surface and continuous posture corrections.       Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness      Isaac Sim supplies props and contact geometry; Isaac Lab organizes observations, rewards and reset distributions. Equal observation dimensions do not guarantee compatibility: the jump policy repurposes a command field as a launch trigger.    Define a skill’s boundaries  Walking continuously accepts velocity commands. A kick is a short skill with a start and an end. Integrating it into an autonomous task requires entry conditions, a defined exit state, and a way to stop when conditions are unsafe.      Skill  Observations and actions  Rewards and completion      Jumping  Body state and a jump command → joint actions  Height, landing posture and recovery    Basketball balance  Robot and ball state → joint actions  Balance, relative position and survival    Walking  Body state and velocity command → joint actions  Speed tracking, stability, energy and smoothness        Why ONNX files are not interchangeable  ONNX is a model representation, not a universal robot-skill protocol. The walking model takes 61 inputs, while the kicking residual takes 62. Both output 14 numbers, yet they are not interchangeable. Input ordering, additional state, action scaling, teacher blending, and termination conditions are all part of the runtime contract.  Use the  model inspection commands in Chapter 7 , then record input and output shapes. A readable model file does not guarantee a correct action: units and joint ordering must also match. The fixed task entry point pairs weights with their runtime contract.  Watch the kick in three phases: before it, inspect ball and support-foot positions; during it, identify whether contact comes from the foot or another body part; afterwards, inspect recovery of support. Pause the video in each phase and describe the entry and completion conditions. This is more informative than asking only whether the ball moved.    Describe a skill by its contract  Describe a skill using entry conditions, observations, actions, and exit conditions. A kick requires a useful right-foot ball position, goal alignment, stable support, and fresh target information. Execution combines the kicking teacher with a residual correction. It must then return to a stable standing or walking state; touching the ball alone does not finish the task.  A residual adds a constrained correction to an existing action. This reduces what must be learned from scratch but inherits the teacher’s operating range. Starting a local kick far from the ball does not make it search or approach. Navigation creates a valid handoff state; the skill performs its local action.   Check your understanding  The robot is beside the ball, but its remembered position has expired. Should the kick start immediately?   Show explanation  No. Observe again and confirm the entry conditions. Proximity alone does not guarantee valid inputs.      Executing a skill is not completing a task  These policies already use joint and IMU feedback for balance. They do not yet decide where the football is, which route to take or when to kick. The next chapter designs that external-perception and planning chain.

title: Design the autonomous football pipeline
text:
Turn manual decisions into a system  This chapter follows the walking-shot pipeline: visual localization, Nav2 planning, walking approach, kicking and recovery. Chapter 7 adds a separate visual-feedback roller branch that contacts the ball directly without walking sole odometry or a kick actor.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Autonomous football data flow  Sensors：RGB / ToF / IMU / joints；Detection：Image → ball / goal；Geometry：Pixels and pose → location；Kick stance：Goal direction → pose；Approach：Nav2 path → body velocity；Motion and checks：Walk / kick → observation        Isaac Sim: acquire and interpret sensor data   Planning and execution: goals become actions        Sensors  RGB / ToF / IMU / joints   Detection  Image → ball / goal   Geometry  Pixels and pose → location   Kick stance  Goal direction → pose   Approach  Nav2 path → body velocity   Motion and checks  Walk / kick → observation    At every stage, identify the data source, coordinate frame, freshness and recovery behavior.       Stage  Input  Method or model  Output      Detection  Isaac Sim RGB images  Object detector  Ball/goal boxes, classes and confidence    Target localization  Pixels, intrinsics, head joints and posture  Geometry and object-size constraints  Timestamped relative target positions    Range and posture  VL53L8CX 8×8 ToF and IMU  Validity checks and orientation estimation  Range sectors, posture and valid flags    Kick stance  Ball, goal direction and kick offset  Geometry; no new neural network  Target position and heading    Route and approach  Map, current pose and target stance  Nav2 Navfn and approach controller  Path and body velocity commands    Motion skills  Body state and velocity/kick command  Walking ONNX, kick teacher and residual  14 joint targets    Coordination  Stage outputs and timestamps  State machine and readiness checks  Walk, re-observe, kick or stop      Not every stage needs a learned model. Detection and motion use networks; geometry, path planning and task transitions can use explicit algorithms. Isaac Sim connects the scene and sensors; Isaac Lab trains and evaluates motion skills.    Three complementary sources      Source  Information  Limitation      RGB  Target location in the image  Does not directly provide metric distance    ToF  Ranges across 64 forward sectors  Invalid sectors cannot be treated as free space    Body IMU  Body orientation and angular velocity  Does not locate the ball or goal      The RGB detector finds image regions resembling a ball. ToF measures ranges across an 8 × 8 forward-facing grid; it is not a 360-degree lidar. A body IMU estimates attitude so image rays and ranges can be interpreted in the right frame. No single sensor supplies the complete world state.  The simulation uses GC2093 camera and VL53L8CX ToF profiles. Images are processed at 960 × 540 and 15 Hz. Lens field of view and noise settings are simulation assumptions; physical devices require calibration.    From a pixel to a spatial ray  Let a detection center be pixel (u, v), with camera focal lengths (fx, fy) and principal point (cx, cy). In a common camera convention, the viewing ray is proportional to ((u−cx)/fx, (v−cy)/fy, 1). This gives direction but cannot distinguish a small nearby object from a larger distant one. Range or a known geometric constraint is still needed.  Camera coordinates commonly use x right, y down, z forward. Here the body convention is x forward, y left, z up. Transform using the camera’s rotation and translation relative to the body rather than mixing same-named axes. Head motion changes this transform, so localization requires joint state at the appropriate time.  An 8 × 8 ToF grid does not provide 64 independent object labels. One cell may cover both floor and ball, and close reflections may be invalid. Check measurement status and range before associating a return with an image target. Treating an invalid reading as an obstacle-free direction gives navigation a false premise.    A past observation can become stale  After moving or tilting its head, the robot may lose the ball from view. Odometry can update a remembered relative position briefly, but error accumulates. Stale observations, invalid ranges, or lost ground constraints require stopping and reobserving. Missing data is not free space.   Check your understanding  If a ball box is accurate, can its center be used directly as a world coordinate?   Show explanation  No. Pixels give an image direction. Spatial position also requires a camera model, camera pose, and distance or geometric constraints.      The ball center is not the destination  The task is to strike the ball toward the goal. Sending the body to the ball center risks premature contact or an unusable approach. Work backward from the kick: face the goal, leave space behind the ball and offset the body to align the kicking foot.   Standing behind the ball is a human-designed task prior.  The designer encodes the shooting direction, robot geometry and skill operating range. The walking network does not infer football rules. Detection learns appearance and motion policies learn actions; geometry computes the stance and Nav2 plans toward that supplied target.  Distinguish relative offsets from map coordinates. A stage may use fixed stand-off and lateral offsets, while its target coordinates change with the ball position or shooting direction. The indoor task uses a visually estimated ball position plus explicit map priors for the known goal and field bounds; it does not discover an entire unknown pitch.    Compute the target position and heading  Express ball B and goal center G in the same planar frame, in meters. Unit vector u points from ball to goal; n points left when facing that direction. Heading is measured counterclockwise from the map +x axis.   Shooting direction and left normal  \[\mathbf u=\frac{\mathbf G-\mathbf B}{\|\mathbf G-\mathbf B\|},\qquad \mathbf n=\begin{bmatrix}-u_y\\u_x\end{bmatrix}\]    Target stance and heading  \[\mathbf P^*=\mathbf B-d\mathbf u+\ell\mathbf n,\qquad \theta^*=\operatorname{atan2}(u_y,u_x)\]   Here d is the stand-off and ℓ is the body’s leftward offset. At the target heading, the ball should lie at about (d, −ℓ) in the body frame. Thus B = P* + d u − ℓ n; rearranging gives the target formula. Positive ℓ places the body left of the shooting axis and the ball to its right, aligning a right-foot kick. Reject coincident B and G because the direction is undefined. Stand-off d / m   Left offset ℓ / m   Ball B: y / m   Goal G: y / m      Hold d and ℓ fixed and move the ball or goal; observe P* and θ*. Then vary the offsets. These sliders compute planar geometry, not Nav2 or physics, and do not certify the skill at every value.   For B = (0.02, 0), G = (0.68, 0), d = 0.22 and ℓ = 0.035, u = (1, 0), P* = (−0.20, 0.035) m and θ* = 0°. The body is 22 cm behind the ball and 3.5 cm left of its axis. Moving the ball changes both the direction and target; these map coordinates are not a permanent kick location.    Python · geometry excerpt  Full source ↗    delta = [a.goal[i] - a.ball[i] for i in range(2)]
length = math.hypot(*delta)
direction = [x / length for x in delta]
normal = [-direction[1], direction[0]]
target = [
    a.ball[i] - a.distance * direction[i] + a.lateral * normal[i]
    for i in range(2)
]    This is the core of Chapter 7’s  plan  geometry exercise. The full entry also checks finite values, positive stand-off and distinct points. It outputs coordinates and a diagram, without requesting a navigation path. The next question is whether known space admits a route to this target.    How Nav2 turns a target into a path  Nav2 is an open-source ROS 2 navigation framework. This task uses its Navfn planner: a start pose, target pose and costmap produce a sequence of path points. The task rules above supply the target; Nav2 does not understand right-foot kicking. See the  Nav2 source project .  An occupancy grid distinguishes known free space, obstacles and unknown cells. A costmap adds traversal costs, with higher costs near obstacles to encourage clearance. The robot has a footprint, so checks must consider an envelope around the path, not a zero-width line.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram                                           
 
  
 R  P*  Teaching example: a hypothetical obstacle  Blue: planned path; dashed circle: approximate robot footprint    White: known free space; dark gray: obstacle; tan: higher cost near the obstacle; gray: unknown. R is the start and P* the goal.  This hypothetical obstacle illustrates costmaps. It is not a measured map from the empty-field experiment or a Navfn search replay. Unknown cells are not free space, and a route still requires footprint and execution checks.   The configuration explicitly enables A*. Its intuition is to compare candidates using the cost already incurred plus an estimate of the remaining cost. The conceptual formula below explains goal-directed search; it is not a line-by-line description of Navfn’s potential updates and path extraction.   Conceptual A* score  \[f(n)=g(n)+h(n)\]   Here g(n) is the accumulated cost to candidate cell n, and h(n) estimates its remaining cost. These scalar search symbols are separate from goal G and the normal vector in the geometry section. The search method is selected by configuration, not learned by the walking network.    YAML · Navfn configuration excerpt  Full source ↗    planner_plugins: [GridBased]
GridBased:
  plugin: nav2_navfn_planner::NavfnPlanner
  use_astar: true
  tolerance: 0.025
  allow_unknown: false
  use_final_approach_orientation: false    Unknown-space planning is disabled.  tolerance: 0.025  is the path-end tolerance in meters, not a foot-to-ball tolerance. The 4 × 3 m navigation grid at 2.5 cm resolution is distinct from the physical 1 × 1.6 m mat. The 0.10 m circular footprint is a navigation approximation, not a substitute for bipedal motion and contact validation. See the  Navfn parameter reference .  The full task submits an immutable snapshot of timestamped observations, known field bounds, robot pose and target to a ROS 2 Jazzy Nav2 service in a separate CPU container. The bridge publishes the matching map and transforms, then calls  ComputePathToPose . Returned results must match the request, coordinate frame and map snapshot. ToF observations and known empty-field priors do not establish unknown-scene mapping or general obstacle avoidance.    How does the robot execute the approach?   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Planning and execution in this task  Nav2 and checks：Map and target → path / permission；Task controller：Vision, posture and stage → command；Walking policy：Body command → 14 joint actions       Planning and execution in this task     Nav2 and checks  Map and target → path / pe  rmission   Task controller  Vision, posture and stage   → command   Walking policy  Body command → 14 joint ac  tions    Motion changes relative position; new observations update targets, commands and stopping conditions.   A conventional Nav2 stack can use a controller server to follow a path and publish velocities.  This task does not enable that full execution chain.  Its bridge obtains Navfn paths and traversal checks; a custom controller combines visual ball bearing, stance error and posture to generate bounded turning, forward, alignment or stop phases. The video does not show a stock Nav2 controller following every waypoint.   From body commands to joint actions  \[\mathbf c_t=(v_x^{\rm cmd},v_y^{\rm cmd},\omega_z^{\rm cmd}),\qquad \mathbf a_t=\pi_{\rm walk}(\mathbf o_t,\mathbf c_t)\]   Body commands express desired motion. The walking policy combines them with proprioception to produce 14 joint actions at 50 Hz; Newton advances physics at 200 Hz. Commands are not measured achieved velocities: gait, contact and delay introduce error, requiring feedback. Use the executor’s conventions for turning signs and velocity scaling.   Implementation: why stages use different distances       Stage  Ball-relative parameters  Purpose      Nav2 preparation target  d = 0.22 m, ℓ = 0.035 m  Target of the base controller’s path request    Coarse-approach permission  d = 0.36 m, ℓ = 0.028 m  Checks a straight segment; no additional Navfn search    Near-ball observation stance  d = 0.26 m, ℓ = 0.035 m  Preparation for observation and alignment    Nominal final stance  Ball at about (0.09, −0.035) m in body coordinates  Fine alignment followed by kick-readiness checks      These belong to different control layers; they are not four map waypoints that every run must visit in sequence. Validate changes against the skill’s operating range. Kick readiness also requires the ball within body-frame x∈[0.075, 0.105] m and y∈[−0.05, −0.02] m, plus valid observation age, heading, posture and head return.  Compare the  base target and path handling ,  coarse checks ,  visual stage control  and  final approach and readiness region .        Check  Evidence to inspect  What remains unproven      Path produced  Matching request, valid path, unknown-space and footprint checks  The robot has reached the target    Preparation stance reached  Position/heading error, stable posture, fresh observation  Immediate permission to kick    Kick readiness  Near-ball region, heading, freshness and head handoff  A guaranteed goal    Complete success  Physical ball crossing and recovery under scoring rules  Success from other initial conditions       Check your understanding  Nav2 returned a valid path, but the robot is still turning. Has it reached the kick stance?   Show explanation  No. A path is a planning result. Check actual position, heading, posture and observations, then kick readiness separately. A motion command is not evidence of arrival.      How do Isaac ROS and Nav2 relate?  Nav2 is an independent open-source navigation framework, not an NVIDIA proprietary navigator. Isaac ROS provides NVIDIA-accelerated ROS components that can supply perception, localization and environmental representations to Nav2. For example, Visual SLAM can provide poses, and nvblox can reconstruct an environment from depth and poses for use through costmap interfaces. Call this  Isaac ROS integration with Nav2 , rather than treating them as one product.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Optional Isaac ROS + Nav2 architecture  Camera and pose inputs：Meet calibration and timing needs；Isaac ROS components：Visual SLAM / nvblox, for example；Nav2：Use pose and environment for navigation       Optional Isaac ROS + Nav2 architecture     Camera and pose inputs  Meet calibration and  timing needs   Isaac ROS components  Visual SLAM / nvblox, for  example   Nav2  Use pose and environment  for navigation    This is an optional architecture, not the current task implementation. Check sensor, compute and synchronization requirements for each component.    This task uses Isaac Sim with ROS 2 Nav2; it does not currently use Isaac ROS packages.  Isaac Sim renders RTX sensor data, Isaac Lab organizes learning tasks and policy interfaces, and Newton advances physics. CPU-hosted Nav2/Navfn plans while a custom controller handles stages and commands. Using Isaac Sim does not imply Isaac ROS integration. Inspect the  package lock  and  service source .  For physical deployment or more complex fields, first identify whether localization, mapping or control needs improvement, then select components and validate interfaces, delay and task outcomes. The  official Nav2 vision-navigation tutorial  shows integration with NVIDIA components; its sensor and compute setup is not automatically available on Microduck.    Approach in stages    1 Search and observe   2 Coarse approach   3 Fine alignment   4 Check kick conditions   5 Kick and recover   At a distance, reducing range is the main priority. Nearby, motion must become more precise while preserving visibility, heading, and foot placement. Being close enough is not sufficient if heading is wrong.  A planner supplies a route or direction; the walking policy executes it. A valid planned path does not prove the robot has traversed it. The system must handle tracking errors, contact, and sensor updates.      Focus on approach and stance adjustment: control relative position and heading, not just apparent ball size.     Work through a stance target  Subtract the ball position from the goal center and normalize the result to obtain the shooting direction. The stance lies behind the ball: move back by  distance  along that direction, then sideways by  lateral  to allow space for the kicking leg. This exercise defines its own offset convention; it does not replace calibrated entry values in the physical skill.  First run the  stance geometry command in Chapter 7 . Open  plan.svg  to inspect the stance, ball, and goal.  plan.json  gives the target position and heading. Change distance from 0.18 to 0.25 with a new output directory; predict the direction of movement and check it. This command computes geometry from known points. It runs no physics and does not prove reachability.  The full task also handles yaw drift, delayed gait response, and targets leaving view at close range. Approach therefore updates observations and checks stopping conditions repeatedly. If valid range or floor support is lost, stop or retreat within constraints and observe again. Unknown space cannot be declared free space.    When should the robot look again?      A focused view of ball observation and head motion.   A first observation supplies an initial target, but motion changes relative geometry and estimation error accumulates. The current controller verifies position before kicking. Retreat is a recovery option, not a mandatory phase.   Check your understanding  Why not kick at the last known location when the ball leaves view?   Show explanation  Motion changes relative position and the estimate may be stale. Check time, pose and stance before kicking; reobserve when necessary.

Some targets are cropped by image edges: a detection box can exist while metric geometry must reject the incomplete contour and request another view.    Practice training a detector  The command below trains for five epochs on the small practice set so you can inspect loss and detection boxes. Run it from the repository root with a new output directory.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py train-detector \
  --data datasets/scene-sample/dataset.yaml \

  --output outputs/student-detector-01    The small dataset and five epochs introduce data, labels, training, and validation; this is not a full training recipe. Inspect loss curves and validation images. To improve quality, diversify scenes and keep training, validation, and test scenes separate.   Keep the course detector downstream  The detection lab and full task use  models/scene-detector/detector.pt . The 40-image practice subset has 24 training, 8 validation and 8 test images, grouped by scene seed. Practice training does not replace the course model; mAP is not shooting success.     Inspect labels and detections  The sample has 40 images split into 24 training, 8 validation, and 8 test images. Class 0 is the ball and class 1 the goal. Each YOLO label row is  class cx cy width height , with the last four values normalized by image dimensions. A horizontal center of 0.5 means halfway across the image, not 0.5 meters in the world.  Choose one clear prediction and one difficult example. Check missed objects, false detections, and misplaced boxes, then compare object size and position. High confidence cannot repair camera calibration or turn a 2D box into depth. Navigation still requires range, attitude, timestamps, and validity checks.   Check your understanding  Can a ball label centered at (0.6, 0.4) be used directly as a navigation target at (0.6 m, 0.4 m)?   Show explanation  No. These are normalized image coordinates. A camera model and range or ground constraint are needed to obtain robot-relative position.      What must adapt when the scene changes?  Domain randomization exposes a model to meaningful variation during training. Apply it to the affected component: mat colours, markings, light and mesh affect RGB detection; friction, voltage, delay, mass and contacts affect locomotion and kicking. This system combines detection, geometry, Nav2 and action policies; it does not use a vision-language-action model such as GR00T.  This exercise fixes the goal shape, size and material. Visual variation covers two football surfaces, marble, wood, illumination, ball position and camera pose. The motivation resembles varying tube placement and colour for GR00T, but this system uses separate detector and motion policies; only the detector was fine-tuned for this scene, and GR00T is not used.   Check your understanding  Recall the  slope-walking training in Chapter 4 . Does adapting Microduck to different slopes count as Domain Randomization? Does this implementation also use Curriculum Learning? Identify evidence for random variation and difficulty adjustment before revealing the answer.   Show explanation   This course's training uses both terrain domain randomization and curriculum learning, but training on several slopes alone would not establish that.    Where is the randomization?  The training entry point defines 5 difficulty rows and 8 terrain columns: 2 flat, 3 pyramidal and 3 inverted pyramidal. Types are assigned by proportion, not randomly drawn each episode. When generating the terrain, each tile receives difficulty  d = (r + u) / 5 , where the row index is  r = 0,…,4  and  u  is sampled uniformly from [0, 1). The slope parameter's magnitude is  0.03 + d × (0.22 − 0.03) . This is  tan(α) , not degrees; the configured range corresponds to about 1.7°–12.4°. Random variation in slope geometry at generation time qualifies as terrain domain randomization. A new slope is not drawn from the entire range at every reset.   Where is the curriculum?  Training sets  curriculum=True  and  max_init_terrain_level=1 , and retains the rough-terrain task's  terrain_levels_vel  update. Environments start at randomly assigned level 0 or 1. At resets, levels change according to horizontal displacement from the environment origin: above 2 m advances a level; otherwise, displacement below the current translational command magnitude × episode time limit × 0.5 lowers the level. Levels are bounded below by 0; advancing beyond the highest level assigns a random level. Difficulty therefore adapts to performance, rather than following a fixed iteration schedule from flat ground to steep slopes.   How do they differ?  Domain randomization concerns random variation in training environments; curriculum learning concerns how difficulty is scheduled. They can be combined. Testing fixed straight ramps at 0, ±5°, ±10° and ±15° in Chapter 4 is an evaluation protocol, not domain randomization by itself. This classification also does not establish a real-world performance benefit from randomization alone.  Check the implementation:  training configuration ; the course-pinned Isaac Lab  terrain sampling ,  promotion and demotion criteria , and  level assignment .        Variation  Main effect  Response      Surfaces A–D, light, camera pose  Boxes and contours  Generate varied RGB data; split by scene    Goal size/location and ball diameter  Metric scale, map and scoring  Update geometry contracts, not only textures    Friction, voltage, delay and mass  Gait, impact and recovery  Measure ranges; test whether policy adaptation is needed    Unknown obstacles, edges or deformation  Traversability and contact  Extend sensing/physics and then test planning/control      The official black-and-white ball, its diameter, the sloped-back goal and new surfaces change the visual input. On the same 128 new test images, the previous indoor detector scores mAP50 0.379, with ball AP50 only 0.020. We therefore fine-tune the detector while preserving walking, kicking and residual weights. The dataset has 48 scene seeds and 768 images; all surfaces and views sharing a seed stay in the same split.  The detector was fine-tuned for 60 epochs using 512 training, 128 validation and 128 test images. Held-out mAP50 is 0.978 and mAP50–95 is 0.934. These measure detection quality, not autonomous task success or the isolated benefit of randomization; that requires a matched-data, matched-budget ablation. Localization, paths, kicks, goal crossing and recovery require separate task tests.  Let failures determine whether to widen randomization. Test one fixed model on all four surfaces, then on unseen lighting and ball positions. Lost ball contours near white lines point to perception; correct recognition and stance followed by slip or failed recovery point to dynamics. Avoid changing every parameter at once, which obscures the cause.  Check your understanding: can lighting randomization fix localization after widening the goal but keeping the old centre spacing and map? No. Converting pixels to metres depends on the actual dimensions; correct the geometry contract first.  This fine-tuning run used 60 epochs and about 4.8 minutes of training wall time, excluding collection, export and complete simulations. Appearance and light variation target perception. Changing known goal dimensions also requires matching localization priors, maps and scoring, or a separate method that estimates unknown dimensions.      Same 128 held-out indoor images  mAP50  mAP50–95      Previous indoor detector  0.379  0.314    Adapted detector  0.978  0.934      This comparison supports adapting the detector to the new scene. It compares old and adapted models, not training with versus without randomization, so it does not isolate a causal randomization benefit. Better detection still leaves observation freshness, path handoff and recovery to validate.    Check stance geometry first  Review  stance geometry  and  Nav2 planning . Run the command below from the repository root on CPU, with a new output directory. It checks geometry only; it does not start Nav2 or the robot.    Terminal  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py plan \
  --ball 0.08 0.03 --goal 0.68 0 \
  --distance 0.18 --lateral 0.035 \
  --output outputs/stance-plan-01    Inspect  plan.svg  and compare with the previous chapter’s equations. This exercise checks geometry with supplied points. The full task estimates ball and robot positions, combines them with the known goal’s map prior, and then invokes navigation and motion skills.  Expected: P* ≈ (−0.0980, 0.0739) m and θ* ≈ −2.86°.  distance  is the stand-off along the shooting axis;  lateral  is the leftward offset, both in meters. Inspect  plan.json  and  plan.svg , then change only the ball position and use a new output directory. Explain the target change. The full scene submits real Nav2 requests; a returned path still requires motion and readiness checks.    The teacher and residual in walking shots  The course kick combines a fixed base policy with a trained residual model. The residual adjusts the base behavior, so observations, action scale, actuators, and timing must match. Removing one model does not leave an equivalent skill.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-teacher.onnx
python3 scripts/workshop.py inspect-model --model models/kick-residual.onnx    Find both files in the model inventory. Compare their input and output shapes and distinguish robot-state inputs from task inputs. The complete task uses the pair in Chapter 7; retraining is not required here.    Understand the complete walking-shot system  This is not a single network issuing a “score” command. A walking policy controls the body, a detector supplies visual targets, range and attitude constrain relative position, a state machine decides when to observe, walk, and kick, and the kick models execute contact and recovery.    1 RGB + ToF + IMU   2 Target estimates   3 Navigate and align   4 Fixed kick models   5 Task evaluation       One complete direct-shot example. The inset shows the actual robot camera synchronized with the full scene. One demonstration is not a success-rate estimate.     Run the complete teaching scene  Run the command below from the repository root to start autonomous football. Use a new output directory for video, sensor records and scoring.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --scene indoor --style A --record-hd \
  --seed 983102 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-01    Expected result: an Isaac simulation window opens and one robot searches, approaches, aligns, and attempts a kick autonomously. The program uses the repository’s fixed models and saves video, traces, and results. The 180-second budget is simulation time, not wall-clock waiting time. Initialization and rendering can take longer.  This seed is a selected teaching fixture drawn from successful examples. It supports comparison on the same scene and is not a new independent success-rate sample. Do not manually move the robot or ball during execution. To stop, press Ctrl+C in the terminal and retain the logs.  The indoor fixture starts the robot at (−0.55, 0.04) m and ball at (0.02, 0) m, with the goal plane at x = 0.68 m. Robot and ball coordinates initialize the scene; goal position and dimensions are known map priors. Runtime robot and ball positions still come from sensor estimates. Select patterns with --style B, C or D, and change starts with --root-y or --ball-xy. Record altered conditions as separate tests.    Judge complete walking-shot success  After the preceding run, read its score with the command below. Change  --run  if you used another output directory.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01     A real foot–ball contact occurred.  The entire ball crossed the goal plane inside the opening.  The robot did not fall or exceed the specified mechanical bounds.  There was no premature ball contact, and the robot recovered after kicking.    Interpreting the reference result  The original simple field and narrower goal completed 9/10 independent tasks. That historical result does not transfer to the marked mat, steel-mesh goal and full-body contacts. The current A-pattern demonstration completed contact, whole-ball crossing and recovery in 32.565 task seconds, passing all 11 applicable checks. It is a development example, not an independent success-rate estimate. New pattern tests must remain separate.       Surface / seed  Complete task  Task time  Fall      A / 55001  Failed  10.755 s  No    B / 55002  Failed  29.165 s  No    C / 55003  Failed  60.000 s  No    D / 55004  Failed  60.000 s  No      Four predeclared seeds at the same start, one per surface with a 60-second task limit, completed 0/4 full tasks. Passing record audits is not task success. Surface and seed change together, so these trials do not isolate a surface effect or estimate broad reliability. They use the 10 cm ball and remain separate from historical 7 cm tests. See the  current scene trial records .  All four failures preceded the kick: A failed the current-body guard during handoff recovery and its ball observation then expired; B could not reacquire a complete ball observation during fine approach and stopped at the attention deadline; C did not obtain valid complete ball geometry; D did not obtain the required consecutive goal-base observations. C and D reached the 60-second task limit. None fell. Inspect geometry, field of view, observation age and planning handoff before deciding what additional training data are needed; these trials do not establish a failure of the walking or kicking policies.    Gliding shot: observe, make contact and stop early  The gliding task uses the same 10 cm ball, goal, camera and detector. It loads the official roller actor from initialization to the end. Its wheels are passive, with propulsion and braking produced by leg motion. Wheel–ball contact transfers momentum without switching to walking or executing a leg kick. The fixed start is about 30 cm behind the ball: this tests short empty-field approach and shooting, not navigation from arbitrary field positions.      Complete gliding example: camera observation, physical contact at 6.79 s, whole-ball crossing at 8.13 s and settling before the goal. Initialization, contact and the ending all remain in roller mode. The observer view is re-rendered from this episode’s physical record, synchronized with its original camera frames. This development example is separate from the independent trials below.   The controller detects the goal and ball and estimates approach direction from pixels, camera geometry and a ToF ground plane. It slows, aligns and gradually returns head control to the roller actor. After settling, it propels briefly and adjusts braking using estimated velocity while remaining on its wheels. Waiting for perception also requires coasting control: releasing propulsion is not a stop.   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Gliding-shot control sequence  Observe：RGB + ToF: ball and goal；Approach and align：Slow down and check direction；Prepare contact：Release gaze control, settle, propel；Brake early：Ball rolls; robot settles       Gliding-shot control sequence      Observe  RGB + ToF: ball and goal   Approach and align  Slow down and check  direction   Prepare contact  Release gaze control,  settle, propel   Brake early  Ball rolls; robot settles    Detections guide approach and preparation. Physical records independently determine contact and scoring; the controller does not read simulator ball coordinates.   This visual-feedback branch does not integrate Nav2 or walking sole odometry. Braking velocity is integrated from ideal trunk-COM specific force, gyro and gravity-direction measurements, starting at zero velocity. The controller does not read true robot velocity or ball coordinates. IMU mounting offsets, bias and vibration are not modeled, so this is not a hardware stopping solution. The command below uses the evaluation configuration: no window or additional live observer recording, while still rendering RGB/ToF and saving sensors, actions and physics. Watch the full demonstration above and use a new output directory per run. A fixed seed does not guarantee success.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --locomotion rollers --seed 42 --style A \
  --headless --no-record-hd \
  --seconds 40 \
  --output outputs/football-rollers-01    Inspect the result with the command below. Complete success requires physical contact, whole-ball crossing, no fall throughout the episode, and at least one continuous second settled before the goal at less than 2 cm/s. Detection or contact alone is insufficient. Results retain contact and crossing times and the final continuous settling duration.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report \
  --run outputs/football-rollers-01        Floor / new seed  Goal  Full task  Outcome      A / 56001  Yes  Failed  Post-shot settling deadline exceeded    B / 56002  Yes  Passed  Contact, scoring and stopping passed    C / 56003  No  Failed  No valid two-post-base observation    D / 56004  No  Failed  No valid two-post-base observation      With models and control parameters fixed, four predeclared new seeds, one per floor, completed 1/4 full tasks and scored 2/4 goals; none fell. Runs have a 30 s ceiling and an 8 s settling deadline after the propulsion/contact window. A continued moving after scoring; C and D waited for valid goal geometry until the limit without propulsion. Surface and seed change together, so these small samples do not isolate a surface effect. Improve post-base extraction and braking consistency; a higher detection score alone is insufficient, and these trials do not establish that the roller actor needs retraining. See the  gliding-shot records .  Consider why the roller push command is not a target speed. If the wheel grazes the side of the ball, why might a larger push make the outcome worse? Inspect contact direction, head-to-body handoff and braking before deciding whether policy retraining is necessary.    Design a small evaluation  Write down seeds and success criteria before running. Record goals, falls, contact, and recovery for every episode. Do not replace a failure with a retry. A model or parameter change defines a separate experiment.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py football \
  --seed 990001 \
  --seconds 180 \
  --output outputs/football-new-seed-01     Check your understanding  Why can the task fail even when detection mAP is high and the walking policy stays upright?   Show explanation  Success depends on interfaces between modules. Targets can leave view, coordinates or observation age can become unsuitable, and position or heading may fail the kick conditions. Module metrics do not replace end-to-end evaluation.      Locate a problem from a failed run  First check the result file:  result.json  for walking or  independent-result.json  for rollers. If not, inspect the terminal error and installation or runtime conditions: that is an execution failure. If results exist, distinguish failure to find the ball, failure to reach a kicking stance, contact without a goal, and failure to recover after scoring. A normal process exit does not mean the robot completed the task.  For walking,  course_evaluation.passed  combines physical scoring and applicable checks.  scorer  retains contact, goal crossing, and fall information. In synchronized views, inspect the stance before first contact and posture after kicking. A short clip of the ball crossing the line is insufficient for a full-task judgment. For rollers,  autonomous_task_passed  marks complete success; wheel contact, whole-ball crossing and continuous settling are reported separately.  The original simple-field combination completed 9/10 independent tasks. The new mat and steel goal change appearance, geometry and contacts, requiring separate evaluation. Default seed 983102 demonstrates the new scene; repetitions are not independent samples.

title: Recap and a harder football challenge
text: From skills to a complete task   Scroll horizontally to view the full diagram    Learning through eight chapters  Experience：Keyboard → robot structure；Train and transfer：Flat → slopes → skills；Act autonomously：Sensing → planning → goal       Learning through eight chapters     Experience  Keyboard → robot structure   Train and transfer  Flat → slopes → skills   Act autonomously  Sensing → planning → goal    Isaac Sim provides an observable, resettable world. Isaac Lab organizes experience collection, policy learning and evaluation into reproducible experiments.       Capability  What you have done      Use skills  Load official ONNX actors and issue keyboard commands    Understand the robot  Inspect joints, load paths, sensors and control timing    Train skills  Collect parallel experience, update PPO and export an actor    Test generalization  Compare flat ground and slopes under matched conditions    Complete a task  Connect perception, localization, planning, walking and kicking      A motion actor solves how to move. A complete system also decides what to do, where the target is, whether information is reliable and when to switch skills. Keep demonstrations, skill benchmarks and task-level evaluation distinct.    Challenge: slopes, uneven ground and obstacles  Suppose the pitch has slopes, uneven patches and obstacles. Can the robot still score? This is a design challenge only; it is not implemented in the course.      Change  Questions to investigate      Slopes  Can the actor balance? Does the ball roll before contact?    Uneven ground  Is projection onto z = 0 valid? Is local surface height or depth needed?    Obstacles  How can a map provide clearance and support replanning?    Inclined kick surface  Are the flat-ground starting pose, ball relation and recovery conditions still valid?    More complex task  How can perception, navigation and motion failures be separated?      Draft a one-page proposal: scene variables, sensors, reusable policies, new training needs, data splits, success criteria and compute budget. Use Isaac Sim for scenes and Isaac Lab for terrain and skill evaluation.    One final question   Check your understanding  Why do slope walking and flat-pitch shooting not establish slope-pitch autonomous shooting?   Show explanation  The combined task changes ball motion, localization assumptions and kicking conditions. It needs its own end-to-end evaluation.

title: Troubleshooting
text:
Start with the environment report  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py doctor
python3 scripts/workshop.py verify-models    The first failure is more useful than repeatedly launching a full training run. Check the repository directory, the selected runtime, and all model checks.    Common issues      Symptom  What to check      No GUI window  Use the GPU desktop terminal and check DISPLAY and the driver. A remote text shell is not a graphical desktop.    First launch is slow  Check for downloads and compilation. Allow initialization and avoid starting duplicate instances.    Output directory exists  Choose a new run name and preserve the previous result.    Out of memory  Reduce training environments or detector batch size. Avoid concurrent simulations.    Model hash mismatch  Restore the repository model and check for accidental overwrites.    Practice policy walks poorly  A short run teaches the workflow. Inspect reward, episode length, and evaluation. Continue with fixed models.    Robot stops or does not score  Inspect the task report and observation validity. Stopping can be appropriate when information is missing; it is not a goal.        Inspect a run  Run the command below in a terminal at the repository root. If it specifies an output directory, use a new one to retain earlier results.    Terminal · Bash  Copy command    python3 scripts/workshop.py report --run outputs/football-01    When reporting an issue, include the command, seed, environment report, and first error. A success/failure label alone is not enough. Do not include passwords or access tokens.

title: Further learning and references
text: Robotics and simulation  Begin with task observations, actions, and rewards, then explore physics and sensors. Course commands target fixed versions; current documentation may describe newer versions. Check the version before applying changes.    Suggested extensions   Vary the Chapter 3 training budget and compare on the same unseen seeds.  Add backgrounds and lighting conditions to Chapter 5 and evaluate generalization.  Visualize Chapter 7 target positions and headings for different ball locations.  Predefine new seeds for Chapter 7 and retain all successes and failures.
